author: dereuromark
body:
Implements carve-js's half of `markup-carve/carve#963`, the PART 7 clause `ONE WHITESPACE DEFINITION, IN EVERY CONSTRUCT`.

Whitespace means space, tab, carriage return and line feed. Every other C0 control, vertical tab and form feed included, is CONTENT in every construct.

## The ticket's carve-js premise was stale

It named three rows: a trailing form feed dropped from a heading, the same from a caption, and a lone vertical-tab line read as blank. **All three are already correct on `main`** - carve-js's headline half merged as `markup-carve/carve-js#883` earlier today, and the ticket's table was written before that.

Re-measured rather than read. What remains is wider than the ticket implies: **fourteen further constructs, twenty-two divergent rows**, found by sweeping every site that classifies a whitespace run rather than by working the named list.

That ratio is the repository's usual one. The tab rule was stated five times and was stated twelve; the fence class named three sites and had eight; the abbreviation budget named three and had five.

## Two rows are correctly wide and stay

The link destination, per PART 3, and quote flanking after a non-breaking space. Both are pinned by control mutations, so a later sweep that "aligns these with the rest" fails rather than quietly narrowing them.

## Proof

Sixteen named mutations. Fifteen kill at least one case. The sixteenth is diagnosed rather than dropped: it has no observable effect on any input, so no case can pin it, and that is stated instead of a case being invented to look like coverage.

Every control character in every fixture is built from an escape and its bytes asserted before use. Three probe files on this ticket silently lost a literal U+000B when written and produced three wrong readings; that is why the assertion is there.

## Scope

carve-js only. `markup-carve/carve#963` stays OPEN - carve-php still owes its half. Corpus rows are owed and are named on `markup-carve/carve-php#1038`; they belong in the spec repo, not here.

author: alexyakunin
body:
Fixes the sidebar chat list jumping backwards on fast mobile scrolls when contact data isn't cached.

> **Note:** the second commit (`fix(rpc): stop PushStream logging a spurious delay timeout`) is unrelated to the split — it was already in the working tree and is carried here at the author's request. Reviewable independently.

## Root cause

Finite mode sized its whole coordinate system from `statistics.itemSize` — a **cumulative mean that never resets**, over a sample weighted by how often each item happened to resize (`addItem` is only called from the `ResizeObserver` path):

1. On a fresh load only the first measured batch informs it, and that batch isn't representative — measured **78 px** against a true average of ~56.
2. The wrapper is sized `count * itemSize` (`virtual-list.ts:2041-2042, 2080`), so with N=402 every drift pixel is multiplied by hundreds.
3. Fast scrolling measures many rows at once, so the mean falls in steps (78 → 57.6) and the wrapper follows: **14 changes, −9018 px total, one single step of −5740 px**.
4. A shrink landing while the viewport is near the bottom pushes `scrollTop` past the new maximum and the browser clamps it — **a 700 px jump backwards**, measured in one frame with zero user input.

Slow data is what makes it visible rather than imperceptible: fling far and a big batch of rows gets measured in one go, so the mean moves in a step instead of drifting.

## Approach

The two lists wanted very different machinery behind one component, so they're split rather than the estimate patched.

```
VirtualList.cs            abstract base — data-source round trip, JS bridge, item visibility
├── FiniteList            ChatList
└── InfiniteList          chat view, content tabs, log view
```

**`FiniteList`** — known length, uniform item height, real scrollbar:

```
top(i)      = i * itemSize
startSpacer = firstLoadedIndex * itemSize
endSpacer   = (N - lastLoadedIndex - 1) * itemSize
wrapper     = content-driven — no explicit height write at all
```

Loading a different window cannot move what is on screen, so the no-jump invariant is **structural rather than maintained**. `itemSize` is measured from a designated row instead of estimated: `IVirtualListItem.HasRegularSize` (false for `ChatListItemModel.IsLastItemInBlock`, the pinned-block separator) projects to `data-vl-size-source` on the `li`. Nothing averages, so nothing drifts.

**`InfiniteList`** — the former `VirtualList`, behaviour unchanged, with `IsInfinite` and every finite branch deleted. All of them were dead when `isInfinite === true`, so the infinite path is equivalent by construction.

**`VirtualList`** — abstract base. `InfiniteList.razor.cs` 182 → 32 lines, `FiniteList.razor.cs` → 24.

## Also in here

- **`RequestDataTimeout` 800 ms → 2500 ms**, and it now warns when it fires. `endRender`/`renderSkipped` already cover both normal outcomes of a completed round trip, so the timer is a fault backstop, not flow control. At 800 ms against slower-than-800 ms data it fired on *every* request, silently degrading the in-flight guard from "one request at a time" into "a new request every 800 ms".
- **New `scroll-clamp` check.** `anchor-jump`/`render-jump` measure `Δtop + Δscroll`, which is identically 0 when the browser clamps — structurally blind to exactly this bug. The signature is deliberately narrow (range must shrink, scroll must go backwards, result must be pinned at the new max) because `InfiniteList` has several scroll-write paths and only one stamps `lastProgrammaticScrollAt`; a looser test produced 4 false positives per fling.
- `/virtual-list-debug` skill rewritten for two components, plus the per-frame tracer used to validate this.

## Validation

402 chats via `/bot-army`, iPhone-class emulation, `debugDataLoadDelayMs = 2500`, hard flings both directions:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| scroll clamps | 1 × −700 px | 0 |
| wrapper changes | 14 (−9018 px) | content-driven |
| idle frames with on-screen movement | — | **0 / 503** |

Repeated with deliberately non-uniform row heights (the condition that broke the old implementation): same result. `scroll-clamp` verified against four synthetic cases — fires on a real clamp, silent on scroll-without-resize, shrink-far-from-the-end, and range-grew.

Chat view regression-checked throughout: loads, scrolls, sticks to the bottom, item count grows correctly on scroll-up.

## Review notes

- **No TypeScript base was extracted.** Only ~47 lines are genuinely shared (DOM ref resolution, `parseRenderState`, `getItemRef`, the request guard, the instance registry) against 2700 + 400 lines of deliberately different machinery. Coupling the two lifecycles to dedupe that cuts against the point of the split. The C# base is where the real duplication was.
- **Blank viewport on very fast scroll is unchanged** and still expected — out of scope by design.
- Two subtleties are documented in the skill because they will bite again: a Blazor render arrives in *several* batches so `endRender` must gate on the render-state JSON's own `renderIndex`; and the scroll anchor must be captured in the rAF read phase, not on scroll.

author: ttraenkler
body:
A boxed **constant** number is immutable and its identity is not observable (see below), so one module global initialised once is indistinguishable from a fresh box per call. This hoists them.

## Census and size

Acorn 226 KB self-parse, lane `standalone-dynamic`, checksum 422 on every build:

| | before | after | Δ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **boxed-number allocations** (`type_67`) | 3,862 | **0** | **−3,862** |
| all allocations | 215,286 | 211,424 | −3,862 |
| the other 25 allocation streams | — | — | **byte-identical** |
| `__box_number` calls | 556,923 | 490,598 | **−66,325 (−11.9 %)** |
| binary (`standalone-dynamic`) | 1,544,411 B | 1,543,371 B | **−1,040 B (−0.07 %)** |
| binary (dogfood standalone acorn) | 937,273 B | 936,139 B | −1,134 B |

The allocation delta is *exactly* the whole boxed-number stream and *exactly* nothing else.

**Binary size goes down, which was not guaranteed.** 49 globals plus a 148-instruction seed block cost less than the 697 `f64.const`(9 B) + `call`(2 B) pairs they replace with a 2–3 B `global.get`. Break-even is ~3 sites per distinct constant; acorn averages 14. A toy module with one site per constant *grows* (measured 435 → 485 B). **No minimum-use threshold was added on purpose** — the site count is *static*, and the highest-value case here is the opposite shape: 12 static `Infinity` sites executing 3,862 times.

No wall clock is quoted. #4216 priced the entire helper at ≲2 % of parse, so nothing here is resolvable on this box.

> **Baseline note:** these were measured before #4217 landed (hot/cold split now default-ON). The **absolute binary figures will have shifted**; the census delta will not — it is exactly the boxed-number stream, which the split does not touch. Stated rather than silently re-quoted.

## The identity question — checked, and it found something

*Can anything observe that two boxes of the same number are different objects?* **No, for every constant except `NaN`** — and the reason is the interesting part:

- For i31-able values **shared identity is already the regime**: `ref.i31` is not a heap object, so two with the same payload are already `ref.eq`-equal. #3673 puts 99.31 % of boxing there.
- Every consumer compares boxed numbers **by value**, and each was written that way *because* distinct boxes of equal values exist. `__extern_strict_eq` (`any-helpers.ts:634-660`) takes `ref.eq` as a fast path but **explicitly excludes** the `$BoxedNumber` carrier and falls through to `f64.eq`. That exclusion (#3174) exists precisely so `NaN === NaN` stays false for the same reference.
- Sharing can only flip an identity test false→true, which for every constant but `NaN` is the answer the spec already requires.

So **`NaN` is excluded from hoisting.** It buys nothing — #4216's census found *no* NaN in the constant population, which was entirely `Infinity` — and it removes the only case where sharing is a semantic risk rather than a semantic improvement.

## Design call worth knowing about

The globals are seeded by `__module_init` **calling `__box_number`**, not by a constant init expression. `ref.i31` / `struct.new` / `extern.convert_any` are all valid constant instructions, so the const-expr form was available — but it would have required this pass to re-derive #3673's i31-ability rule (integral, in `[-2^30, 2^30-1]`, not `-0`), i.e. a second copy of a rule that lives in `registerNative("__box_number", …)` and is silently wrong the day the two drift. Cost of the chosen form: a three-instruction flag test per `__module_init` entry.

## A test-design note, recorded in the test file

The first fixture **had no top-level state**, so the module had no `__module_init` to seed from, the pass correctly bailed, and ON/OFF produced **byte-identical binaries** — a parity-only test would have passed while measuring nothing. The test now asserts the binaries *differ*, pins the per-iteration slope of both censuses (4 boxing calls/iteration → 0, allocations −3, control function untouched), and checks answers against **native Node** rather than against the OFF build.

## Gates

`equivalence-gate` **exit 0, no new regressions** — 24 failing, all in the 36-entry baseline; 12 baseline entries now pass (not ratcheted here). Dogfood canaries **2/3/4/5**, `functionImports: []`, exactly the 3 pre-existing IR-FALLBACKs, all matched against a baseline measured on the same tree first.

`tsc`, prettier, biome, oracle-ratchet, loc/func budget (allowance in the issue frontmatter for `index.ts` +8), stack-balance, any-box-sites, coercion-sites, ir-fallbacks — all exit 0, **each read from its own log rather than a pipe**.

## Relationship to #4216

|---|---|---|

author: mizzy
body:
Closes #3708

## Problem

`scripts/check-docs-use-new-spellings.sh` was a dead guard, for three independent reasons (see the premise-correction comment on the issue):

1. **Dead patterns** — `\b` in awk ERE is a literal backspace (BSD awk and gawk alike), so neither pattern could ever match. Feeding the script's exact awk a ` ```crn ` fence full of old spellings exits 0.
2. **Not wired** — no CI job and no pre-commit hook ran the script.
3. **Fence-tag anchoring** — only ` ```crn ` fences were scanned; README tags its DSL blocks ` ```hcl `.

Additionally, the resource pattern required a `(ec2|s3|iam|sso|logs|sqs)` service segment, so the spellings that actually rotted in README before #3707 (`aws.vpc`, `aws.security_group.ingress_rule`) would not have matched even a live version.

## Fix

- Rewrote the patterns as POSIX ERE without `\b`, and added a service-less lowercase-path pattern that catches the `aws.vpc`-era spellings while accepting current PascalCase type paths (`aws.ec2.Vpc`) and their snake_case enum value tails (`aws.ec2.Vpc.InstanceTenancy.dedicated`).
- Scan every fenced block regardless of tag. Only fences explicitly tagged as a known non-DSL language (rust, json, yaml, toml, ts/js variants, python, go) are exempt — their native syntax (`x: bool`, `: string`) collides with the patterns, and nobody tags Carina DSL as rust. A DSL block mis-tagged `hcl`/`text`/untagged is still scanned, so the failure direction is safe. URLs (`https://aws.amazon.com/...`) are excluded via a `/` left guard.
- The script now accepts explicit file arguments (for tests); default mode still walks `git ls-files '*.md'` minus `notes/`.
- New `scripts/test-check-docs-spellings.sh`: 12 checks proving the guard **fails** on each old-spelling class — including the literal pre-#3707 README excerpt and an old spelling *after* an exempt fence (pins the fence state machine) — and passes on current spellings, prose outside fences, AWS URLs, Rust fences, and a repo-wide default-mode run. This makes the dead-guard state itself a CI failure.
- New `Docs Spelling Check` CI job runs the self-test, then the check.

## Verification

- TDD red run recorded: the test script against the original checker fails 5 of 8 checks (all bad fixtures sail through); green after the rewrite (12/12).
- `bash scripts/check-docs-use-new-spellings.sh` on the current repo: exit 0 (no false positives; earlier drafts flagged `super::arn()` in docs/plans and `carina-provider-aws*.git` URLs, fixed via context guards).

body:
Closes `P35f` and `P35g`. Ships as **v11.1499**, flagged a behavior change.

## The defect

The tool taxed heirs on capital gains that IRC §1014 wipes out, in two places:

1. **First death.** The surviving spouse's cost basis carried straight through the `MFJ → SGL` flip with no reset, so every later sale from that account realized more gain than it really would.
2. **Final death.** Terminal wealth was valued as `basis + max(0, brokerage − basis) × (1 − capGainsRate)` — a liquidation, not an inheritance.

The error ran **one way**. Roth and Cash were unaffected, so every comparison between converting and not converting leaned toward converting, through Break Even, `bestConversionStopYear`, the ⚓ baseline pick and every "Optimize for" ranking. Nothing measured on top of it was trustworthy, which is why this blocked P36 round 2.

## Measured effect

| | Baseline | After |
|---|---|---|
| Default plan, ending wealth | $625,885 | **$637,024** |
| Default plan, lifetime tax | $561,705 | **$551,192** |
| Default plan, spending | $4,467,103 | $4,467,103 (identical) |

Brokerage-heavy plans move ~11.6%. Controlled pair TX vs FL — both no-income-tax states, differing *only* in `BasisStepUp`: **+$184,854** wealth, **−$127,539** tax. A single filer's wealth rises while lifetime tax is **unchanged**, which is the proof the two step-ups are correctly separated.

## Design decisions that changed the recorded spec

- **No `deathBasisStepUp` enum, no knob, no `'none'`.** Step-up is a function of law, not preference. Goldens were rebaselined rather than kept green behind an escape hatch.
- **Not a `COMMUNITY_PROPERTY` list.** A separate list is a second place to forget when P19 adds a jurisdiction. All 38 modelled jurisdictions carry their own numeric `BasisStepUp`; a test asserts every one declares it, and that the community-property set is exactly `AZ CA ID NV TX WA WI`. `NO_TAX_SHELL` holds 0.50 with `NV`/`TX`/`WA` overriding **after** the spread.
- **Terminal row only**, not every year — wealth at death is not wealth now.
- **Break Even deliberately unchanged**, on the liquidation basis. Lifetime break-even and legacy-basis break-even are different questions; the second gets its own phase.

## The trap this is built around

A `_cfRun` counterfactual completes fully. Without a guard, its last row reaches the Break Even block **already stepped up** while the main log's has not, and the final year's `convOC` differences two different valuations — silently, with no error, moving reported break-even years.

Avoided structurally, not by care: the post-pass sits **after** the BE block *and* skips on `inputs._cfRun`. Verified by isolation — a build with the terminal step-up disabled produces a **bit-identical** `convOC` series.

## Two findings, not just rebaselines

- **The T6 divergence is back.** `optimizer_core.tests.js` recorded that `finalNW` vs `baselineScore` divergence vanished with the double-credit fix, that a 64-variant search failed to reproduce it, and that its regression guard was lost. The step-up restores it exactly — same mechanism shape, a real asset instead of phantom cash. Those tests are divergence guards again.
- **`CONV_BASE`'s time-limited conversion was an artifact.** Worth $1,221–$5,587, against a $28,551 modeling error favouring *not* converting. Moved to `TL_BASE` with a larger IRA, deliberately keeping the brokerage gain so the test clears the correction rather than dodging it.

## Also in this PR

- **P35f**: `Basis <= Brokerage` invariant, plus removal of a dead `optimizer_ui.js` line that assigned an undeclared global `basis` instead of `BrokerageBasis` and had never fired.
- **Chart**: death markers carry a drawn half/full glyph (Unicode has no same-size pair — U+25D0 inks 9×7, U+25CF 6×4); the final death is marked at all, where **single filers previously got no death marker**; the `i % 3` label stagger now tests real pixel extents, fixing collisions that predate this work. Overlapping label pairs: 1 → **0** on the default plan.
- **README**: the "there is no basis step-up" limitation replaced with four named residual limits (LA/NM unmodelled, aggregate basis with no per-spouse attribution, AK opt-in, no loss carryforward), each with its direction of error.

## Verification

`node optimizer_core.tests.js && node taxPaymentPlanner.tests.js && node doclinks.tests.js` → **222 / 32 / 22**, up from 214. Browser badge **518 green**. Browser-verified: basis steps at the first single year and again at the terminal row, CA's jump is exactly 2× CT's, the legend tracks the state, and Break Even is unmoved.

author: satish-krishna
body:
## What this does

`[permissions] mode = "prompt"` now enforces, verified against a live claude session. The work splits enforcement between the two mechanisms by what each can actually reach:

- **`allow` / `deny` → a generated claude `--settings` file.** Claude enforces them natively. Kata no longer matches rules at all.
- **`unmatched` → Kata's MCP `approve_tool`.** Anything the rules leave unresolved reaches Kata, where the policy decides or the run pauses on the operator.

Proved live, one run, both halves:

```
git log --oneline -3              -> DENIED   (settings-enforced rule)
cp README.md .kata-split-probe.txt -> PAUSED on the operator, exit 123 on the deadline
```

`git log` is the important one. It is **read-only**, and claude auto-approves those without consulting any prompt tool — so a deny living in Kata's own matcher was silently inert for exactly the calls a deny most needs to cover. Moving the rules into settings fixes that.

## Why it took this shape

This branch began as "the Workbench surfaces for prompt mode shipped untested — cover them." That found five real bugs, three of them already shipped. Then running it against a real claude found the sixth and largest: the arbitration wasn't firing.

The investigation established claude's actual evaluation order:

1. settings **deny** → refused (prompt tool never called)
2. settings **allow** → permitted (prompt tool never called)
3. **read-only command set** (`git status`, `git log`, `cat`, `ls`) → auto-approved, prompt tool never called
4. otherwise → `--permission-prompt-tool`

Two conclusions follow, and the design is built on them: rules written into settings pre-empt the tool entirely, and rules held only by Kata can never see a read-only call. Neither mechanism dominates, so each now does the job it can do.

Keeping the rules in one matcher — claude's — also removes the risk of two implementations of the same grammar drifting apart. Kata's grammar *is* claude's grammar; the arrays are handed over verbatim.

## Bugs fixed along the way

1. The approval card's **Deny button rendered near-white on the dark theme** — bare `.k-btn` has no background and inherited the browser default. Shipped that way.
2. The allow-rules placeholder used `
` entities, which Svelte collapses — a field labelled "one rule per line" showed one line.
3. `api.submitDecision` fabricated a `permission.decided` for a request that could never arrive.
4. The demo timeline scripted a pause its own deny rule would have swallowed.
5. The demo claimed an `allow-rule` match that anchored matching rejects.
6. The demo scripted `decided_by` values the engine cannot emit.

(4), (5) and (6) share a shape worth naming: **the tests were green the whole time.** A fixture can pass and still teach something the engine cannot do.

## Also in here

- **Permission cards and ask panels render inline**, spliced back where the pause happened, instead of piling at the end of the transcript. Mutation-tested: restoring the docked behavior fails all five ordering tests.
- **Test coverage went 85 → 128.**
- Two dev papercuts where the documented commands failed on a clean checkout (`npm test` didn't run `svelte-kit sync`; `cargo test --workspace` needs the sidecar staged).
- Bidirectional drift pointers between the Rust validators and their TypeScript mirror — the absence of which is why the mirror went stale in the first place.

## Contract note

`decided_by` narrows: `allow-rule` and `deny-rule` can no longer occur, leaving `unmatched-policy`, `operator`, and `engine`. `permission.decided` is therefore no longer emitted for calls a rule resolved — claude settles those and Kata never sees them. Any claim of a *complete* audit trail is removed from the docs rather than softened.

`CONTRACTS.md` explicitly declares the `decided_by` value set **not frozen**, and requires consumers to treat an unrecognized value as "something else decided it". No event type or field is renamed or removed, so `protocolVersion` stays at **1** and the crate version stays at **1.1.0**. `docs/consuming-kata.md` states what a consumer must stop relying on.

## Test plan

- [x] `cargo test --workspace` — 165 unit + 36 integration + 19 CLI, 0 failed
- [x] `npm test` — 128 tests across 17 files; `npm run check` — 0 errors
- [x] `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- [x] Both JSON schemas and the ts-rs bindings regenerate with no diff
- [x] All 10 example katas validate
- [x] **Live against real claude:** deny refuses a read-only command; an unmatched call pauses on the operator and hits the answer deadline at exit 123
- [x] Driven in the desktop app: the approval card renders, the verdict crosses the bridge, and the approved call executes

author: patrickkumar27
body:
## Problem

On K-pop / hip-hop (e.g. Enhypen — *Fatal Trouble*, ~117 BPM) the counts run **~2x too fast**. The tempo detection is correct (not an octave error) — the issue is that the app puts a count on *every* beat, while dancers count these genres in **half-time** (one count per two beats).

## Change

Adds a `beats_per_count` knob:
- `1` = a count on every beat (full-time) — **default, output unchanged**.
- `2` = a count on every other beat (half-time).

Count "1" still lands on the detected downbeat. In half-time, `beat_timestamps` / `counts` describe the **count positions** (every other beat), which the frontend already consumes as `(timestamp, count)` pairs — so no frontend change is required to try it.

## How to use

- Globally: set `BEAT_SYNC_BEATS_PER_COUNT=2` in `backend/.env`.
- Per request: `detect_beats_and_sync(path, out, beats_per_count=2)` — lets the route expose a per-video half-time toggle later.

## Not covered here

This fixes the **speed** ("2x too fast"). It does **not** fix the **downbeat placement** ("1 and 8 land on the wrong beat") — that's a separate phase problem addressed by running the LLM (vs the heuristic) and/or a re-anchor control.

## Verified

Count-position math unit-checked: full-time output is byte-identical to before; half-time yields half as many counts with "1" on the downbeat.

body:
#234 was merged before it could be reviewed, and its five new preview classes reintroduce both faults fixed earlier today. This restores the invariants; no test coverage is lost.

## 1. Paths — the captures were outside the compared root

All five wrote to a literal `"screenshots/previewApp/…"`. Since #229 that is not where the comparison looks. Images are matched **by their path relative to `SCREENSHOT_ROOT`**, so a capture written elsewhere is not a *differing* image — it is one with no counterpart, and it silently stops being compared.

It also recreated `composeApp/screenshots/`, the directory #229 emptied and gitignored, which is how **32 PNGs came to be committed again**. Routing the five through `SCREENSHOT_ROOT` fixes both symptoms at once, and the images are removed.

## 2. Naming — CI never ran any of them

`AppPreviewAboutTest`, `AppPreviewContactTest`, `AppPreviewConverterTest`, `AppPreviewSetupWizardTest` and `AppPreviewStatisticsTest` do not contain the substring `ScreenshotTest`, so the workflow's `--tests '*ScreenshotTest*'` never selected them. CI rendered none of them and compared none of their images — they could have passed indefinitely while testing nothing.

This is the same defect #228 fixed for the previous batch, and `AGENT.md` records the rule.

## Verification

Ran CI's exact command. All five now appear in the recorded set:

```
AppPreviewAboutScreenshotTest
AppPreviewContactScreenshotTest
AppPreviewConverterScreenshotTest
AppPreviewSetupWizardScreenshotTest
AppPreviewStatisticsScreenshotTest
```

**204 images** are generated under `build/screenshots`, where these five previously contributed none. `composeApp/screenshots/` is not recreated by a record run. Full suite green.

## Worth considering separately

Both faults are easy to reintroduce because nothing enforces them — the naming rule lives only in a comment, and a stray path literal fails silently rather than loudly. A test asserting that every `AppPreview*`/`*Screenshot*` class matches the filter, and that no capture lands outside `SCREENSHOT_ROOT`, would turn both into a build failure instead of a review catch. Happy to add that if you want it.

author: shurrman
body:
## What

The release workflow built native packages only for Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora and Arch. The existing `macos` job was a portability check only: it built from the release archive and produced no distributable artifact.

This adds a `macos-package` job that produces a real macOS release:

- **Matrix over architectures**, each built natively:
  - `macos-latest` (Apple Silicon, arm64)
  - `macos-15-intel` (Intel, x86_64)

  Homebrew libraries are architecture-bound, so each architecture is compiled on its own native runner instead of cross-compiling a universal binary.

- **Full plugin set**, with Samba and MongoDB required rather than auto-detected.

- **Self-contained runtime** under `/opt/mc6`: `dylibbundler` collects the Homebrew dylibs used by `mc` and every panel plug-in, install names and runpaths are loader-relative, every modified Mach-O is ad-hoc signed, and `magic.mgc` is included with an explicit runtime path. Homebrew is a build-time dependency only.

- **Deliverables**: an unsigned and unnotarized `.pkg` installer and a `.dmg` that carries it, named `mc6-<version>-macos-<arch>.pkg/.dmg`.

- The artifacts are named `macos-<arch>-packages`, so the existing `publish` job picks them up via the `*-packages` pattern and attaches them to the draft release alongside the `.deb`, `.rpm`, and `.pkg.tar.zst` files.

The fast `macos` check job remains separate.

## Validation

- Clean arm64 configure/build/install from the current merged branch, with Samba, MongoDB, S-Lang and libmagic required.
- `make check` passes.
- Every staged Mach-O is checked with `otool`, has no `/opt/homebrew` or `/usr/local` Homebrew dependency/runpath, and passes `codesign --verify --strict`.
- The staged binary runs with `TERM=xterm`; CI additionally hides the complete Homebrew prefix before that smoke test.
- The generated `.pkg` contains `/opt/mc6`, both required plug-ins, the bundled dylibs and `magic.mgc`.
- The generated `.dmg` passes `hdiutil verify`.
- Workflow YAML parses cleanly.

## Notes

- The installer package is not Developer ID signed or notarized. Browser-downloaded builds may be blocked by Gatekeeper until explicitly allowed in Privacy & Security.
- The Mach-O files inside the package are ad-hoc signed after all `install_name_tool` changes so they are executable on arm64.
- Run `/opt/mc6/bin/mc`, or add `/opt/mc6/bin` to `PATH`.

body:
## Summary

- unify hook- and provider-resolved decisions under one validated lifecycle
- discard null or invalid hook decisions and continue to later hooks or the provider
- require exported `AfterHookMeta` with the exact resolving hook or provider source
- support layered cache warming without rewriting the resolving cache
- harden `dedupeHook` ownership, rejection, finalization, and follower-timeout behavior
- export `HookResolutionAbortError` for third-party single-flight hooks
- document the lifecycle contract and add a minor changeset

## Why

Hook-resolved decisions previously skipped after hooks, which could orphan dedupe requests. Invalid or stale cached decisions could also force perpetual defaults instead of reaching the provider. The unified lifecycle keeps hook ordering correct, validates decisions before after hooks observe them, and allows exact resolver identity to guide cache writes.

Null cache misses now fall through to the provider, while custom single-flight hooks can deliberately abort the resolve chain when a shared evaluation fails.

body:
↩ **[Change 0259 — Harden render-board: sanitize feeder values and settle the failure contract](https://github.com/danielhanold/docket/blob/docket/docs/changes/active/0259-harden-render-board-sanitize-feeder-values-and-settle-the-fa.md)**

Gives `scripts/render-board.sh` a closed, loud failure contract. Malformed change files are rejected **by vocabulary, before their values can reach a TAB join or an associative-array subscript**, each is diagnosed on stderr, and a non-zero count exits **3** so every caller stops trusting a corrupt render.

Consolidates #0155 (interior TABs shift the archive feeder) and #0156 (exit 0 on corruption).

## What changed

**Five rejection classes, one closed enumeration.** M1 unusable id · M2 empty status · M3 status outside the seven-name `DOCKET_STATUSES` vocabulary · M5 a path containing TAB/CR — all in one upfront pass; plus M4, an archive-feeder **round trip** (join the tuple, split it back with the consumer's own `IFS=$'\t' read`, require every field unchanged).

Rejection-by-vocabulary *is* the sanitization: a control-character value can never match a closed name, so it never reaches a feeder. `sanitize()` is used only on the diagnostic surface.

**Deliberately not malformed:** a vocabulary-valid status in the "wrong" directory (legitimate mid-sweep state — stays `board-row-dropped`'s territory), unknown/absent `type:`, malformed `created:`.

**Exit codes:** `0` clean · `2` CLI-argument error (unchanged) · `3` malformed change file(s).

**The accepted cost, stated plainly:** one malformed file anywhere freezes `BOARD.md` and halts autonomous selection until a human fixes the named file. That is spec Assumption 1, deliberate — corruption-adjacent state should stop the loop loudly rather than run beside an unrenderable backlog. See the results file's *Verify (human)* items.

- New: `docket_status_is_member` in `scripts/lib/docket-frontmatter.sh` — full-vocabulary membership beside its `_active`/`_terminal` siblings.
- `scripts/render-board.md` documents the shipped contract, including the exit-3 row and the M1–M5 table.

## Review

Whole-branch review at the **deep** rung (highest build profile routed was `premium`; the diff was under the 1500-line bump threshold). **8 findings: 1 blocker, 3 important, 4 minor.**

| # | Severity | Finding | Disposition |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | blocker | M4 never evaluated under `--format digest` — the guard sat below the digest's early exit, so markdown exited 3 while the digest exited **0** with a wrong tally, splitting the contract across `board-refresh.sh` and `docket-status.sh` over identical input | **fixed** `27c85f0a` |
| 2 | important | An M4-rejected file was still counted by `ARC_COUNT`, the `<summary>` header and the digest rollup; a fourth `ARCFILES` consumer (mermaid `DONE_IDS`) had no gate at all | **fixed** `27c85f0a` |
| 3 | important | `mark_malformed` emitted the file path raw — M4's own case (a TAB in a filename) wrote a literal TAB to stderr | **fixed** `27c85f0a` |
| 4 | important | The ACTIVE-side `SECTION` feeder had the identical exposure with no guard on any of its four consumers — a TAB in an active filename rendered raw into `BOARD.md` at exit 0, undisclosed | **fixed** `b1615773` (new class M5) |
| 5 | minor | In-script comment said "Two conjuncts" while describing three | **fixed** `27c85f0a` |
| 6 | minor | The `[ ! -e "$f" ]` conjunct turned a benign concurrent file move into exit 3 with a misdescribing diagnostic | **fixed** `27c85f0a` (round trip removed the conjunct) |
| 7 | minor | M4's conjuncts and the SECTION-loop `BAD` gate are unexercised by any test | **recorded** — after M5 they are unreachable *by construction*, so the requested fixture is impossible; retained as defence in depth, labelled in code and contract. Residual risk disclosed in the results file |
| 8 | minor | The validation pass re-read and discarded every field (~16% slower on the live backlog) | **fixed** `f7d44db6` — now ~31% faster than the pre-fix branch and faster than `origin/main`, both projections byte-identical over the 261-file live backlog |

No re-review round after fixes, per the fix-loop contract — remediation rides in this diff for the human to read. No ADR was recorded: the one architectural decision was settled at design time in the spec; the implementation-time choices are documented in `scripts/render-board.md`.

## Notable plan deviations

- **The plan's M4 mechanism was wrong.** `IFS=$'\t' read -r date id st f` assigns the *unsplit remainder* to the final field, so a TAB in a filename lands wholly inside `f` without shifting anything — the plan's two conjuncts left the test red when applied verbatim. Superseded by the round trip.
- **The plan placed M4 at the render-time consumer**, which is what put it below the digest's early exit — the blocker.
- **M5 is not in the plan or the spec**; it was added at review time to close finding 4.

This matches Cargo's behavior.
- Nextest now detects the base output directory for test binaries built from `[[example]]` targets, which Cargo places in `examples` rather than `deps`. Binaries exposed via `CARGO_BIN_EXE_<name>` are still filtered out if no test binaries from that package are selected. ([#​3516])
- The "Archiving" message now counts non-test binaries correctly. Previously, nextest counted the number of packages containing non-test binaries rather than the number of binaries. ([#​3515])

- Nextest now computes the dynamic library search path correctly under [build directory layout v2](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/13/call-for-testing-build-dir-layout-v2/), which became the default on nightly Rust on 2026-07-30. Previously, tests that linked against a `dylib` dependency failed to start because the dynamic library could not be found.
- When Cargo's [`build.build-dir`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html#buildbuild-dir) is configured, nextest now adds the Cargo artifact directory (where final artifacts like binaries and dynamic libraries are uplifted to) instead of the build directory (for intermediate artifacts) to the dynamic library search path. This matches Cargo's behavior.
- Nextest now detects the base output directory for test binaries built from `[[example]]` targets, which Cargo places in `examples` rather than `deps`. Previously, a run restricted to examples didn't add anything to the dynamic library search path, so an example test linking against a `dylib` failed to start.
- While [creating an archive with a filterset](https://nexte.st/docs/ci-features/archiving#filtering-test-binaries-from-an-archive), nextest now always includes dynamic libraries in the archive, even those from packages whose test binaries are all filtered out. Dynamic libraries are on the library search path and may be loaded by tests in other packages. Binaries exposed via `CARGO_BIN_EXE_<name>` are still filtered out if no test binaries from that package are selected. ([#​3516])
- The "Archiving" message now counts non-test binaries correctly. Previously, nextest counted the number of packages containing non-test binaries rather than the number of binaries. ([#​3515])

body:
Layer 0.3 of the adic-spaces roadmap: **the completion of a Huber ring is a Huber ring**, and of a Tate ring is a Tate ring. Wedhorn Remark 6.8, in a new `TauCeti/RingTheory/Huber/Completion.lean`.

Given a pair of definition `(A₀, I)` for `A`, the ring of definition of `Â` is the topological closure of the image of `A₀` (`PairOfDefinition.completionRingOfDefinition`), and its ideal of definition is `Î`, the ideal of `Â₀` generated by the image of `I` (`PairOfDefinition.completionIdeal`). Openness of `Â₀` follows Mathlib's own `Nonarchimedean/Completion.lean` template — `IsDenseInducing.closure_image_mem_nhds` puts the closure of an open subgroup's image in `𝓝 0`, and `AddSubgroup.isOpen_of_mem_nhds` makes it open.

The substance is `IsAdic Î`, and it rests on one identity:

```text
completionIdeal_pow :  Îⁿ  =  closure (image of Iⁿ)
```

`≤` is formal. `≥` is the real content — Stacks 05GG in disguise — and needs a convergent approximation argument. An element of `closure(image Iⁿ)` is approximated to order `Iⁿ⁺ᵏ` at each stage; finite generation of `I` is what makes the *number of terms* in each approximation uniform in `k`, so the coefficient series are Cauchy and converge in `Â`. That is the only place `fg_ideal` is used, and it is why the roadmap carries finite generation in `PairOfDefinition` at all. The argument is factored into five private lemmas — `exists_sum_eq_of_mem_span_mul`, `exists_sub_sum_mem`, `cauchySeq_sum_coe`, `exists_approx_seq`, `completionIdealImageIdeal_le` — so no declaration exceeds 35 lines.

With that identity `isAdic_completionIdeal` is immediate from `isAdic_iff`: each power is open because it is a preimage under `continuous_subtype_val`, and cofinality is `hasBasis_nhds_zero_completion`. Then `PairOfDefinition.completion` bundles the pair and `IsHuberRing.completion` is the instance. `IsTateRing.completion` follows: a pseudouniformiser's image is a unit and stays topologically nilpotent under the continuous `coeRingHom`.

Independently, `ker_coeRingHom` identifies the kernel of the completion map as `(⊥ : Ideal A).closure`, which is the roadmap's "kernel `closure {0}`" bullet.

**What this PR deliberately does not contain.** The roadmap's other two 0.3 bullets — that the completion map has dense image, and that it is a topological embedding when `A` is Hausdorff — are already `UniformSpace.Completion.denseRange_coe` and `UniformSpace.Completion.isUniformEmbedding_coe` in the pinned Mathlib. Restating them here would be duplication, so they are cited rather than reproved. Wedhorn Proposition 6.9(1) (base change) is left for its own PR.

I checked the pinned Mathlib before writing: it has the completion's ring API and an anonymous `NonarchimedeanRing (Completion R)` instance, but **nothing** that transports a subring's closure or `IsAdic` through a completion, and no bridge at all between `UniformSpace.Completion` and the algebraic `RingTheory/AdicCompletion` (the only file relating them, `AdicCompletion/Topology.lean`, relates the *predicates* `IsHausdorff`/`IsPrecomplete`/`IsAdicComplete` to `T2Space`/`CompleteSpace`, not the constructions). Everything generic is reused rather than reproved: `IsDenseInducing.closure_image_mem_nhds`, `AddSubgroup.isOpen_of_mem_nhds`, `Subring.topologicalClosure` and friends, `Ideal.map_pow`, `Ideal.FG.map`, `Filter.HasBasis.cauchySeq_iff`, `cauchySeq_tendsto_of_complete`, `Topology.IsInducing.inseparable_iff`, `addGroup_inseparable_iff`, `IsTopologicallyNilpotent.map`.

Advances `AdicSpaces/README.md` § "Layer 0.3 Completion" (Remark 6.8, and the kernel statement from Proposition and Definition 5.32). author: fastermadman
body:
Closes #32.

PR #44 made abort *honest* for sync jobs (mbsync/bpsync can't stop mid-phase, so it made the wait truthful instead of silent) but deliberately left the harder half open: the registry still rejected any new job until the aborted one finished on its own — no way to force it, no way to start anything else meanwhile, only a server restart.

## Options weighed, and why this one

Reimplementing mbsync/beatport4's own matching logic to get true mid-loop cancellation was considered and rejected again — that's the exact forking-a-third-party-plugin cost the #47/#50 beets-version work just demonstrated firsthand, paid twice over here since it'd mean forking two plugins, not one. Subprocess isolation (the only way to truly hard-kill the call) was also ruled out: it would mean rebuilding the SSE fan-out (`jobs.py`) and the import decision handshake (`importsession.py`) as IPC for every job type, not a #32-shaped change.

Checked before committing to the cheaper option: both network clients already carry real request timeouts (beets' MusicBrainz session defaults to 10s, beatport4's client has its own `HTTP_TIMEOUT`), so a wedged job is bounded in wall-clock time rather than genuinely stuck forever. Draining is sufficient here, not just cheap.

## What changed

- `jobs.start()` now queues at most one job behind an aborted-but-still-running one instead of rejecting it — launched automatically the instant the aborted job's thread actually exits. A second job while one is already queued is still rejected (the invariant stays "at most one job running or about to run," not a general queue). A job aborted while still queued skips its work entirely once its turn comes, rather than running it and ignoring the abort.
- The job panel says plainly that it's waiting ("Waiting for the current mbsync job to finish aborting…") instead of a misleading "Working…" until real progress starts.
- A small header badge (`jobs.queued()` / `/jobs/current`'s new `queued` field) shows *both* halves of a queued pair — e.g. "mbsync aborting · bpsync queued" — since the waiting message alone only exists in the panel of the job that got queued; a different tab, or the same tab after navigating away, had no way to see anything was running. Self-stopping poll: it only ticks while there's something to show, clearing its own interval the instant nothing's running rather than running forever in the background.

## Verified

- `test_jobs.py` (new): synthetic slow jobs exercise the registry's queueing logic directly — reject-while-running, queue-while-aborting, reject-a-second-queue-attempt, auto-launch on completion, and skip-work-when-aborted-while-queued. No beets/Flask/ffmpeg needed.
- `/jobs/current`'s new `queued` field checked through Flask's actual test client against the real route (not just unit-tested in isolation).
- The header badge checked live in-browser against both shapes (running+queued, and nothing running) — renders, hides, and clears its own timer correctly.
- `test_importsession.py` and `test_transcode.py` still pass — the existing import/convert abort paths are unchanged.

> **Model:** Sonnet · **Effort:** medium — bounded fix, options already scoped in the issue and reaffirmed here against facts (the timeout check) rather than just recalled from the original discussion.

author: bong-water-water-bong
body:
Fixes #1527.

## Root cause
The OneBP loader's claimed "dense fallback" was fiction: missing MoE tensors (gu/dn) silently skipped the entire FFN+router (`if (l.gu && l.dn)` with no else), and missing/wrong-sized attention tensors were zero-filled and then *run* — the model loaded "successfully" and emitted garbage logits.

Key finding from the reference implementation (`third_party/llama.cpp/src/models/zaya.cpp`): **Zaya layers alternate** — even layers are CCA-attention only, odd layers are MoE-only ("ZAYA1-8B: 40 sub-blocks (20 CCA + 20 MoE)"). There is no dense FFN anywhere in the architecture; the "dense layer 0" from #1521 is an attention-only layer. The correct behavior for a layer without MoE tensors is to skip MoE — not to fail, and not to run zeroed weights.

## Changes (`src/zaya_engine.cpp`)
- **`load_layer_onebp`**: missing weights → pointer stays null → sublayer skipped (same pattern as the reference `tests/zaya_gpu_decode.cpp`). Present-but-wrong-sized, partial sublayer groups, or a layer with neither sublayer → **abort init loudly** with a per-layer tensor dump for diagnosability. Zero-fill now applies only to optional bias tensors (bias=0 is a correct default; the CCA/router kernels dereference them unconditionally).
- **Post-MLP res_scale fallback**: `res_scale_hs.mlp.*` absent → fall back to `res_scale_hs.*` (llama.cpp reference behavior) instead of zero-fill.
- **`zaya_forward` / `zaya_forward_greedy` / `zaya_forward_batch`**: attention sublayer (incl. post-attn residual scale and the .bin-era pan norm) guarded by `layer_has_attn()`; per-layer pre-norm stays on every layer (matches the graph). The `.bin` path is byte-for-byte behavior-identical (all pointers always loaded there).
- **`zaya_init_onebp` header validation** extended to NH/NKV/HD/expert count — a 24-expert 74B could previously load under a 16-expert config. `intermediate_size` deliberately NOT checked (the converter infers it from the first MoE tensor shape = 2*n_ff rows, not the engine's n_ff; mismatches surface as wrong-sized expert tensors).

## Verification
- New regression check `tests/issue1527_loader_check.cpp` (HIP target): a dense non-Zaya `.1bp` must be rejected loudly. **Passes against `models/Qwen3-0.6B.1bp`** (aborts at `ffn_gate.weight` [3072,1024] ≠ zaya router [1024,256]; previously this zero-filled and "loaded").
- `onebin`, `test_lora_merge`, `issue1527_loader_check` all build clean (gfx1151).

## Notes for #1521 (next validation step)
The strict loader will now also surface the stale tensor-name mapping when a real Zaya `.1bp` exists: real GGUF names are `blk.N.ssm_conv1d` (→ cdw), `blk.N.cca_conv_grp` 3D (→ cgw, needs transpose), `blk.N.ffn_gate_inp` (→ gdw), and the GGUF router has an extra `mlp0` layer the engine's kernel lacks.

author: joshrandall8478
body:
## First: the errors in that screenshot aren't ours

`No marketplace theme installed` and `Class name list not found` are **Marketplace's own Theme Dev Tools** complaining. The first means no theme was installed *through Marketplace* — ours comes from Nix, so that panel has nothing to edit. The second is Marketplace fetching its own class-name list. Neither touches the injection path. The Nord-looking UI in the screenshot is the baked-in `colorScheme`, which is the symptom, not a clue.

## `spotify-theme-doctor`

Spotify's palette travels through four hops and three of them are invisible from a terminal. Every one fails identically — Spotify just stays on the scheme it was built with — which is indistinguishable from the feature not existing. Two rounds have now gone into inferring which hop was down from outside the machine. That's a script's worth of work either way, so here it is:

```
$ spotify-theme-doctor
1. noctalia renders the palette
  ok    ~/.local/state/noctalia-spotify/colors.css exists and is not empty
  ok    it carries the --spice-rgb-* half of the palette
2. the palette service
  ok    noctalia-spotify-palette is running
3. the transport Spotify's renderer uses
  ok    GET http://127.0.0.1:38471/colors.css
  ok    CORS/Private-Network preflight answered 204
4. spicetify injected the script
  ok    xpui/extensions/theme.js carries the injector
  ok    index.html loads it
```

Each `FAIL` says what it means and what to do. It reads the **generation's own package** rather than whatever `spotify` resolves to on `PATH`, so the xpui it reports on is exactly the one this configuration installs — which also catches "you're running an older generation than the fix".

Exercised against a fully broken chain (all six checks FAIL cleanly, exit 1) and a fully healthy one (all pass, exit 0), with the real rendered template and the real palette server.

**If every link is up and Spotify is still wrong**, Spotify has been running since before one of them came up — restart it. Worth checking first that the running generation actually has #61: `spotify-theme-doctor` reporting `preflight answered '501'` means it doesn't.

## GIMP and LibreOffice templates

Both added to `community_ids` (now 13 ids).

**GIMP** is `requires_path`-gated on `~/.config/GIMP`, so it's inert until GIMP is installed and has run once — it costs nothing to list now and starts working by itself later. Same shape as Inkscape and Blender, neither of which is installed here either.

**LibreOffice** is the involved one, and it needs things on `PATH` that NixOS doesn't put in the system profile. Its hook renders an `.xcu`, converts the hex to the decimal integers LibreOffice's `ColorScheme` schema actually requires, zips an `.oxt` and installs it with `unopkg` — so `python3` and `zip` join `jq` in `home.packages`. `unopkg` comes with LibreOffice itself (`home/joshr/office.nix`) and `pgrep` is already there for noctalia.

One behaviour worth knowing, documented in MANUAL.md: the hook **refuses to install while `soffice` is running**, because `unopkg add` against a live install has been seen to corrupt the registration. So a colour change lands on the *second* apply after closing LibreOffice, not on a restart.

- doctor rendered out of the Nix string, `bash -n`'d, and run against both a broken and a healthy fixture
- `community_ids` parsed back out of the file: 13 entries, sorted, matching the intended set
- brace/string balance across all 117 `.nix` files

`nix` still isn't available here, so `nixos-rebuild build --flake .#gamestation-niri` remains the real check.

author: kinfe123
body:
## Problem

With `@assistant-ui/cloud-ai-sdk@0.1.29` and `assistant-cloud@0.1.38`, `useThreads({ includeArchived: true })` made the same unfiltered list call as the default mode. The Cloud `/v1/threads` endpoint evaluates a missing archive filter as `is_archived ?? false`, so a workspace containing one active thread and one archived thread returned only the active thread in both modes.

That server contract is confirmed in `assistant-internal/apps/cloud-api/src/endpoints/threads/list.ts`: both the cursor lookup and the main query apply `eq(threadsTable.is_archived, data.is_archived ?? false)`.

`AssistantCloudAPI` also omits raw boolean `false` query values. Although the current endpoint default still makes that request active-only, relying on the omission hides the intended filter from the wire.

The same backend default exposes a separate archived-thread gap in the older core Cloud adapter. That follow-up is tracked in #5716 and remains outside this focused PR.

## Minimal reproduction

1. Create one active Cloud thread and one thread with `is_archived: true`.
2. Render the hook and refresh:

```tsx
const { result } = renderHook(() =>
  useThreads({ cloud, includeArchived: true, enabled: false }),
);

await act(() => result.current.refresh());
console.log(result.current.threads.map(({ id, status }) => ({ id, status })));
```

Before this PR, the result contains only the active thread. After this PR, it contains both `{ status: "regular" }` and `{ status: "archived" }`, ordered by `lastMessageAt`. The cloneable regression is `packages/cloud-ai-sdk/src/threads/useThreads.test.ts`; run it from this repository with:

```bash
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm --filter assistant-cloud build
pnpm --filter @assistant-ui/cloud-ai-sdk exec vitest run src/threads/useThreads.test.ts
```

## Fix

- request the active and archived status pages separately when `includeArchived` is enabled
- merge both responses by message recency
- stringify `is_archived` in `AssistantCloudThreads.list()` so both `false` and `true` reach the shared query serializer explicitly
- keep the default mode to one active-thread request

The two status requests intentionally fail together: returning only one status while reporting a successful `includeArchived` refresh would silently violate the option and hide an API failure. Existing thread data remains mounted when a refresh fails.

## Verification

- `pnpm --filter assistant-cloud test` (59 passed)
- `pnpm --filter assistant-cloud build`
- `pnpm --filter @assistant-ui/cloud-ai-sdk test` (69 passed with AI SDK v7 and 69 with peer-v6, plus peer-v6 type checking)
- `pnpm --filter @assistant-ui/cloud-ai-sdk build`

## Summary

`pluginStorage.getItem()` was snapshotting the entire database before reading a single value from `pluginCustomStorage`. This changes the read path so only the requested value is snapshotted.

For users with large databases, plugin storage reads no longer need to copy unrelated characters, chats, presets, and other database state just to return one plugin value.

## Related Issues

None

## Changes

- Read the requested `pluginCustomStorage` key directly from the live database.
- Apply `$state.snapshot()` only to the requested value instead of the complete database.
- Keep the existing return behavior for falsy or missing values.
- Keep object and array results detached from the live database state, so plugins do not receive the database proxy itself.

## Impact

There is no database format change and no intended plugin API behavior change. The main difference is the amount of data copied during `pluginStorage.getItem()`: the work now scales with the requested stored value instead of the size of the whole database.

This should mainly benefit long-term users with large character and chat histories, especially when plugins read their storage frequently.

## Additional Notes

This does not change model prompting or response handling. The type-definition checklist item is not applicable because the public API signature is unchanged.

author: tokuhirom
body:
## Problem

```raku
my $d = Encoding::Registry.find('iso-8859-1').decoder();
$d.add-bytes(Buf.new(0xE1, 0xE2, 0xB5));
say $d.consume-all-chars();   # raku: "áâµ"    mutsu: "\x[FFFD]\x[FFFD]"
```

`Buf.decode('latin-1')` was always right — the gap was only in the *streaming* decoder, whose `decode_bytes` special-cased `utf8-c8` and otherwise ran `String::from_utf8_lossy` regardless of the `encoding` attribute it had stored. `consume-all-chars`, `consume-available-chars` and `consume-line-chars` all went through it.

## Fix

- `builtins::decode_bytes_with_encoding_label` — resolves a label through the same alias table `.decode` uses (`latin-1` / `latin1` / `iso-8859-1` are one encoding) and decodes with the existing per-encoding decoder. `decode_bytes` consults it first and falls back to the lossy UTF-8 read only on a decode *error*, which is what a streaming decoder needs for an incomplete trailing sequence.
- `builtins::is_single_byte_encoding_label` — for a single-byte encoding the whole buffer is always complete, so `decode_available` hands it back in one piece instead of running UTF-8's "back off to the last valid sequence" walk, which would have discarded every high byte as an incomplete sequence.

## Effect

Cro builds its HTTP header decoder exactly this way, so any header value outside ASCII was mangled. `t/http-request-parser.rakutest`'s "Field value can be any printable char including latin-1 range" now passes; the file is down to a single remaining failure.

## Tests

- New pin: `t/streaming-decoder-encoding.t` — latin-1 through all three consume methods, plus UTF-8 regression cover including the incomplete-sequence hold-back. Verified against real `raku`. (One case is deliberately not pinned: raku's `consume-available-chars` holds the final grapheme back in case a combining mark follows; mutsu does not, and that is a separate gap.)
- `make test` green (2948 files, 27883 tests).

First step of #77's migration path: `metrics.json` gains a `repo` block — persistence and rework computed over **all authored commits** (everything except automation), cohort-free.

## Why this block exists

The quality-first premise: quality numbers must mean something on a repo where nobody declares anything, because that is the normal case. Today every quality metric hangs off a cohort, and cohorts are empty by default — `No baseline cohort` has fired on every repo we have ever pointed AIDA at.

Two properties, both enforced by tests:

- **Valid at 0% evidence coverage.** All-unknown history → `repo` fully populated, cohort views rightly empty.
- **Immune to the prior.** The `defaultMode` prior may move cohorts; it cannot move these numbers by a single unit (asserted byte-identical with and without). If it could, *"assume everything is AI"* would quietly become *"trust the assumption"*.

Los huecos que quedaban de §8. **En tres de los cuatro el dato ya existía** y se tiraba en la frontera — el patrón de toda esta serie.

## `tipoPrestamoV2` · el «personal» en una hipoteca

Lo escriben el asistente, la importación y la FEIN. **No lo leía nadie.** Una hipoteca dada de alta desde su FEIN llega como `'hipotecario'` y sin garantía apuntada —la escritura se firma después—, así que la cartera la llamaba «personal» teniendo el dato delante.

Orden nuevo: la garantía manda (es lo que firmaste), después lo que el préstamo dice de sí mismo, y solo al final el ámbito.

## La quinta forma de comprobar, que nunca se montó

`SIN_FUENTE` decía «la aportación al plan todavía no se sigue en tesorería». Verdad a medias: **no se sigue en tesorería porque no es un movimiento** — se sigue en `aportacionesPlan`, con su ejercicio fiscal y sus importes. No faltaba el dato, faltaba la pregunta.

La **gestora** pesa tanto como el importe: el anexo no pide un plan cualquiera, pide uno suyo. Aportar a uno de otro banco no arregla nada, así que ahí la respuesta es **«no cumple»**, no «no se sabe» — decir lo segundo mandaría a aportar más a un plan que no bonifica.

Y como el préstamo trae «Unicaja» de su FEIN mientras el plan lo escribió el usuario como «Unicaja Banco, S.A.», la comparación normaliza en vez de exigir que coincidan letra a letra.

## `textoDeCumplimiento` ya sabía decirlo

Sabe explicar cuántos meses de cuántos llegan, qué falta para el mínimo y qué gasto está hecho pero todavía no consta. La ficha nueva lo estaba **reinventando** con un motivo suelto metido en un `title`.

## La pérdida silenciosa de la casilla de seguros

La condición `SEGUROS` admite dos umbrales y la fila del asistente tiene una casilla. Enseñaba siempre el número de pólizas: una condición venida del anexo con **prima mínima** salía vacía, y teclear cualquier cosa borraba media condición sin decir nada. Ahora la casilla habla del umbral que la regla usa, y el sufijo lo dice (`nº` o `€/año`).

## La revisión pendiente vuelve a tener puerta

`revisionPendiente` y `confirmarRevision` llevaban **dos entregas** alcanzables solo desde sus pruebas. El banco revisa, ATLAS no ve su carta, y sin sitio donde apuntar lo que decidió el cuadro se quedaba con el tipo viejo para siempre.

La tarjeta pregunta por cada bonificación —«me la dejan» / «la pierdo»— y por el índice que aplicó. **Nada marcado de salida**: lo que no se conteste se queda como estaba, porque no decir nada de una bonificación no es decir que se perdió. Y el índice vacío es una respuesta legítima: hay cartas que no lo dicen, y entonces se sigue proyectando con el último conocido en vez de fabricar un número.

## Medido

- `solo_tests` **44** · vuelve a donde estaba antes de que se perdiera el cableado
- `alive` **831** · ya no queda ningún módulo de bonificaciones a oscuras

**La procedencia por campo del OCR** (`byField`). Vive solo en `normalize-docai.ts`, que es el camino que sustituyó `leerFeinConClaude`. Añadirle interfaz sería trabajar sobre una vía que se está retirando; lo que hace falta primero es decidir si el lector de Claude debe devolver confianza por campo, y eso es una decisión, no una tarea.

body:
Draft proposal — **nothing here runs**. Make a Claude session declare which project it is working on, and make starting new work in an overloaded workstream deliberate.

📄 [`standard/proposals/wip-gate-for-sessions.md`](standard/proposals/wip-gate-for-sessions.md)

## One disagreement with the ask, up front

You asked for a **pre-commit hook**. I don't think that should be the enforcement point:

| point | when | bypass | reaches mini / Actions sessions |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SessionStart** | before any work | close and reopen | no |
| **pre-commit** | *after* the work | `--no-verify`, silently | no — and absent in a fresh clone |
| **CI on the PR** | after push | changing the workflow | **yes** |

Pre-commit fires after the work it exists to prevent, is trivially bypassed, and doesn't exist until something installs it. A gate that's late *and* optional trains people to route around it.

**Recommendation: SessionStart for the prompt, CI for the enforcement.** Pre-commit is a third copy of the same rule that catches nothing the other two miss.

## Why this is worth doing at all

Reporting is a lagging signal — by the time `the board · Drafts 13/12` shows up on Monday, the work is done. And the survey found **51 open items on no board**, so anything never placed can't be over a limit: the WIP numbers understate real load by whatever that pile is.

Both come from nothing asking *"which workstream is this?"* while the answer is still cheap.

## The part I'd argue hardest for

**The override is recorded, not just permitted** — `Wip-Override: <reason>` as a commit trailer, counted in the Monday review. An untraced override is a bypass with extra steps. And four overrides in a week is a *limit set wrong*, not a discipline problem; the review should say that rather than leave a number nobody revisits.

## Rollout

Warn-only for two weeks first — the same reason the WIP limits were set near current occupancy rather than at an aspiration. Day one must not block the 51 already-unboarded items; the check should **place** work when the column has room, not reject it.

## Open questions in the doc

Per-session or per-branch declaration; whether an override needs approval or just a record; and whether CI should auto-place unboarded PRs (fixes the 51-item gap fast, but writes to boards on every PR — wider than the weekly job's capped 25).

Three of BALANCE.md's open findings, closed.

THE DIVIDEND. Load is now a lifetime measure — it counts every act she has made in this world and does not decay. §2.3's own framing was always a lifetime claim: a world meddled with early and left alone late is still a propped world.

That alone did nothing, and finding out why was the point. The dividend was *gated* on the equilibrium factor rather than banked in proportion to it — `if (eq > 0.5) equilibriumSeconds += dt` — so any load short of the threshold cost exactly nothing, and a light hand and a fairly heavy one banked identically no matter what the load term said. With both fixed, in the shallows Witness banks 20,391 equilibrium-seconds against Interventionist's 1,836, and mints 36 concepts against 16. Restraint out-earns meddling elevenfold.

The opening water worldspace is the exception, for a reason that is content rather than tuning: it is nutrient-poor by design, so restraint cannot produce equilibrium there at all. Both policies bank ~2-3% of a six-hour run — a rounding difference between two failures, not a strategy. Pinned as a test saying so.

THE STUDY MECHANIC. Attention capacity was strictly negative to buy. The fix is Bjork's two strengths, which the observation stages were already halfway to: storage is how deeply she has come to know a thing and never decays — a Known life stays Known, nothing is ever lost — while retrieval is how readily it comes to her now, and does. So a Known life still yields, but yields more when fresh in mind, and returning to it is what freshens it.

The desirable difficulty is the other half: fluency accrues in proportion to how far a thing had slipped, so recovering something half-lost is worth far more than topping up something never allowed to fade. It is permanent, slows all future forgetting, and pays above full recall — without a ceiling to exceed, letting anything fade would be pure loss, which is the opposite of the point.

Capacity is now worth +69% insight over six hours in the shallows. It was -2%.

Not yet demonstrated, and recorded as such: that patience beats grinding. With six slots against eleven life everyone is forced to be patient, so Witness and Patient(0.4) barely differ. The axis only opens at a capacity world 1 never reaches.

LEGIBILITY. The Ledger now names which stocks sit outside their band, so the opening worldspace's permanent "not holding itself" reads as the reason to open the shallows rather than as a bug. Known life cards show recall, and offer the return.

333 tests. The 14 characterization pins that moved are all ones written to catch exactly this kind of change. The perf assertion in sim.test.ts is loosened from 8s to 15s — it is a wall-clock claim about usability, and one that flakes under CI contention is worse than none.

author: dmille6
body:
## The defect

`_dedup` answers *"should this bundle carry the node?"*. A caller about to draw an edge is asking a different question: *"is there a node here to anchor on?"*. Both answers are spelled `None`, and every caller conflated them behind `if obj:`.

Content-addressing turned the collision from nearly unreachable into the common case. Identical values share an id, so the second and every later session in a bundle touching a known CVE, technique, sample, URL or domain got `None` and dropped its relationship. The node survives; what disappears is the per-attacker attribution — the only thing those edges carry.

[PR #43](https://github.com/dmille6/tpot2cti/pull/43) fixed this for Process via `_emit_process`. This generalises that shape.

## The fix

`_emit_node(obj, *, out, node_id)` appends the node when it is new and separately reports the id to anchor on when it already exists in this bundle, with typed wrappers so each type's id derivation lives next to its build call:

`_emit_attack_pattern` · `_emit_vulnerability` · `_emit_file` · `_emit_file_indicator` · `_emit_url` · `_emit_domain` · `_emit_referenced_ipv4` · `_emit_malware`

`out` and `node_id` are **required keyword arguments** — a caller cannot answer half the question by omitting one.

Two normalisation traps the wrappers absorb: `build_url` canonicalises through `valid_url` before hashing, and `build_malware` normalises the family (`"Trojan.Mirai"` → `"mirai"`). Hashing the raw input at a call site would anchor on an id nothing was published under — and only for duplicates, so the first occurrence would still look correct. `_emit_node` logs a `logger.error` if a supplied anchor disagrees with the built object, since that mismatch is otherwise invisible.

## Sites

Eleven converted. Eight came from the review of #43; **three more turned up by sweeping for the pattern** rather than working the list — `build_suricata_alert`'s `http_url` block, its domain-candidate block, and `_build_web_session`'s URL block. That is the argument for one helper over per-site edits.

The three sites that already got the distinction right by hand (`_link_download_chain`, `build_unattributed_payload_objects`' domain, `blocklists`' Feodo family) now go through the same helper, so there is one implementation to keep correct instead of several.

## Measured impact (live graph, 2026-08-07)

| shape | measurement |
|---|---|
| StixFile → attacker edges | 400 most recent: **none has more than one**; 99.2% have exactly one |
| Url → edges | 80 most recent: **max 1**, avg 1.00 |
| Vulnerability → edges | 80 most recent: **all zero**; no `Indicator -> Vulnerability` edge in a 300-edge sample of `indicates` |

A sample dropped by thousands of IPs should not have exactly one attacker edge.

## Verification

- 19 mutations applied one site at a time (revert the guard, run that site's test) — **19 killed**. Two apparent survivors on the first pass were both artifacts of my mutation harness, not test gaps: one ambiguous anchor that mutated the wrong site, and stale `__pycache__` (two mutations landing in the same mtime second at the same byte length, so CPython reran the previous one).
- Tests use two fresh sessions through one builder and assert over the **second**, and go through `ParsedEvent`/`AttackSession.from_event` so `build_cowrie_session` does not return `[]`.
- **885 passing** (863 baseline + 22 new), no regressions.

## Second opinion

`codex` reviewed this before merge. Accepted: ungated `vuln_id`/`ap_id` in `build_unattributed_payload_objects`, and converting the last hand-rolled instance in `enrich/blocklists.py`. Refuted: a claimed double-`out.append(note)` — there is one build and one append.

Codex also flagged a **real pre-existing bug outside this change's scope**: `build_unattributed_payload_objects` anchors its whole salvage graph on `generate_url_id(canon_url)`, which `valid_url` alone does not guarantee `build_url` will emit — the own-surface redaction path can reject it, leaving Sighting/Note/CVE refs to a URL absent from the bundle. Left alone here deliberately (that graph must survive a duplicate URL, and the fix is a product call about own-surface salvage); tracked separately.

Deliberate: the `_emit_*` wrappers stay underscore-prefixed for consistency with `_emit_process`, and `ingest/malware.py` calls them cross-module within the same package, as it already does for `normalize_malware_family`.

body:
Phase 2, module 5 of 6. 44 tests on the fallback — **one real defect, three mistakes of mine**.

## The fallback failed its own validation

The audit called the fallback ladder *the durable protection* around the LLM: this is what an athlete gets when generation has already failed. So a fallback the app itself refuses is the one output it must never produce — there is nothing further to fall back to.

The recovery and taper branches prescribe fixed distances (6 km, 7 km) chosen for a typical athlete, taking no notice of `maxWeeklyRunKm`. **Three of the eight real fixtures — `lowData`, `taper`, `missingHr` — sit near a 12 km cap**, so the plan overshot and `validateWeeklyPlan` returned severity `error`.

Run distances now scale to fit the cap. A **no-op whenever the cap is generous**, so an ordinary athlete's plan is byte-identical. Race week is exempt — the race distance is not ours to shrink.

## Three errors of mine, since the goal asks for them

**My most important test passed vacuously.** It filtered issues by `severity === "high"`, but the validator emits `"error" | "warning"` — the filter matched nothing, so *"the fallback passes its own validator"* asserted precisely nothing. **`tsc` caught it, not me.** Fixing the filter is what surfaced the real defect.

**I claimed `race_week` broke the hard-session cap.** It doesn't. I had forced `planTypeHint: "race_week"` onto a *fatigued, no-race* context whose guardrails said zero hard sessions. No athlete reaches that combination; the real `raceWeek` fixture validates cleanly. The suite now drives every fixture with its **own unmodified guardrails**, which is what found the genuine failures.

**I expected recovery to plan less than build** and read the identical output as a bug. It is the branch order: fatigue is checked above every type except race week, so a fatigued athlete gets a recovery week whatever the caller asked for. Correct — and now pinned, since it is exactly what someone would break while making the hint authoritative.

## How verified

- [x] The V2 fixture gate still passes (84 tests)
- [x] 5 tests confirmed to fail against the pre-fix code

author: sanity
body:
## Problem

**The fleet cannot auto-update.** Since v0.2.120 the node fetches the GitHub release tag and hands it to `semver::Version::parse` **verbatim**, so `"v0.2.121"` fails to parse and every update is silently dropped.

Confirmed on a production node (not inferred):

```
INFO  Startup update check against GitHub current="0.2.120" jitter_secs=20
WARN  Startup update check: failed to parse latest version 'v0.2.121':
      unexpected character 'v' while parsing major version number
```

#5104 changed `parse_tag_from_release_location` to return the tag verbatim — correct for the installer, which builds asset URLs from it — and added `version_from_tag()` to strip. But the stripper was wired into the **installer** path only (`update.rs`). The node's detection path was never updated.

Measured impact: 0.2.120 reached ~85% fleet adoption in 4.6h; 0.2.121 has been flat at ~9-11% for over seven hours. The bug is present in **both** 0.2.120 and 0.2.121, so a fix cannot deliver itself — every operator has to run `freenet update` by hand once.

Tracking: #5221. Post-mortem: #5222.

## Solution

Normalise at the **producer**, in `get_latest_version`, not at each call site.

That function is the node's *detection* path — its own rustdoc says so. Every consumer of it wants a comparable version, never a string that addresses a release. One line at the boundary fixes:

- `compare_versions_for_startup` (the startup check — the site in the log above)
- `check_if_update_available` (the urgent / discovery / version-mismatch triggers, a **separate** broken site that the startup path's tests do not cover)
- the #4073 gates `is_version_pinned_bad` / `is_version_install_gated`

That last one is why the per-call-site fix is wrong. Those gates compare by **exact string equality** against values their writers store **stripped** (`update.rs` `begin_probation` / `record_install_failure`). Fixing only the parses would leave them comparing `"v0.2.121"` against a stored `"0.2.121"`, never matching — silently disabling the crash-loop-rollback pin and the install-failure gate, restoring the restart loop those gates exist to prevent, with no log line.

The raw tag is untouched where a release is **addressed**: `update.rs` still builds asset URLs from `latest_tag`.

## Testing

`get_latest_version_normalises_the_tag` — a **bounded** source pin (the function does network I/O with no injection seam), asserting the normalisation is present. **Verified to FAIL with the normalisation removed**, then pass once restored:

```
test get_latest_version_normalises_the_tag ... FAILED     # fix removed
test get_latest_version_normalises_the_tag ... ok         # fix restored
```

`raw_tag_is_rejected_by_the_consumers` — documents the real failure: a `v`-prefixed tag is **not** detected as an update, while the normalised form is. This is the behaviour that makes upstream normalisation necessary rather than optional.

Full binary suite: 367 passed, 0 failed.

## Why CI did not catch this

The producer's contract and the consumers' contract were each tested, and they **contradicted each other**:

- the producer test asserts the tag comes back **verbatim** (`"v1.2.3"`, with a comment saying so)
- every consumer test injects an **already-stripped** literal (`Ok("0.1.75".to_string())`)

Both passed. Nothing tested the seam. Because both the tag and the version are `String`, the compiler could not object, and the test double was free to drift from the real producer — and did.

#5222 tracks the structural follow-ups: typing the boundary so a release tag and a version cannot be confused (as `release-agent/src/github.rs` already does by returning `semver::Version`), and a release canary that actually exercises **auto**-update — the designated pre-release peer has been running `--disable-auto-update` since 2026-07-29, so the one machine positioned to catch this was configured not to.

## Scope

Deliberately minimal — this normalisation and its tests, nothing else. Every operator must install this release by hand, so a defect means asking the whole network to repeat that. The graceful-shutdown exit-code fix and the `uptime_seconds` fix are ready but held for the next release.

Note on ordering: the exit-code fix must land **after** this one. While this bug is live, graceful-shutdown-exits-1 accidentally fires the unit's `ExecStopPost` hook on every restart, which runs `freenet update` — whose installer path strips correctly and succeeds. That accident is currently the fleet's only working update route, and is the likeliest explanation for the ~10% that have moved.

Fixes #5221
